passages.t: Ephraim's death, and the God who knew him
passages.happening:
‘When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel. But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died’ (verse 1). Now they sin more and more and make cast images from their silver, the work of craftsmen, and people say they kiss the calves (verse 2). So they will be like morning mist, like early dew, like chaff blown from a threshing floor, like smoke through a window (verse 3).

‘Yet I am the LORD your God ever since the land of Egypt; you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me’ (verse 4). God knew them in the wilderness, in the land of drought (verse 5). ‘When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me’ (verse 6). So God will fall on them like a lion, a leopard, and a bear robbed of her cubs (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
The tribe of Ephraim had once been first among the tribes. Joshua came from it, and so did Jeroboam I, the first king of the north. When Ephraim spoke, others trembled. The turn to Baal probably recalls the reign of Ahab and Jezebel in the ninth century BC, when the crown promoted Baal's worship, and Hosea treats that as the moment Ephraim began to die.

Kissing an idol was an act of homage. The phrase the BSB renders they offer human sacrifice is unclear in the Hebrew, and it can also be read as a description of the worshipers: people who sacrifice are kissing calves. Either way, Hosea is mocking the folly of people bowing to animals of their own making. Mist, dew, chaff and smoke all describe something with no substance and no staying power. Houses had no chimneys, only an opening to let smoke out.

Verses 4 to 6 echo Deuteronomy's warning that when Israel ate and was satisfied, its heart would grow proud and it would forget the LORD. The God who knew them in the dry wilderness is forgotten in the green pasture. The lion, leopard and bear were real predators in Israel's hills, and a mother bear robbed of her cubs was proverbial for fury.
passages.later: Moses warned that when Israel had eaten and was satisfied, ‘then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God’ (Deuteronomy 8:14). Isaiah heard the same claim: ‘I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me’ (Isaiah 43:11).
passages.asks: The people forgot God in the green pasture, not in the drought. Ask whether your good seasons or your hard ones draw you nearer to him. And ask what you are tempted to call a savior besides the LORD.

passages.t: Where is your king, and where, O Death?
passages.happening:
‘You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me’ (verse 9), against your helper. Where is your king now to save you, and the rulers you asked for (verse 10)? ‘So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away’ (verse 11).

Ephraim's guilt is bound up and stored away (verse 12). Labor pains come, but he is an unwise son who does not come to birth when the time arrives (verse 13). Then comes a verse read two ways. ‘I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death. Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting? Compassion is hidden from My eyes’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The demand for a king and princes recalls Israel's first request to Samuel for a king, and it may also point to the rapid turnover of northern kings in Hosea's day, when one ruler after another was murdered and replaced. God gave kings in anger and took them away in wrath. The kings Israel trusted could not save it.

Verse 13 uses a striking picture. A child who does not move into the birth canal when labor comes puts both mother and child in danger. Ephraim has the chance to be born anew and will not take it.

Sheol is the realm of the dead. Verse 14 stands out with its address to Death and Sheol, and it sits between verses of judgment on either side.
passages.later: The people had once said to Samuel, ‘appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations’ (1 Samuel 8:5). Paul quotes verse 14 at the high point of his chapter on the resurrection, following a Greek form of the verse: ‘Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?’ (1 Corinthians 15:55).
passages.hard:
Is verse 14 a promise of rescue, or a threat of death?

The Hebrew can be read two ways, and translations differ. Many, the BSB among them, read the first lines as promises that God will ransom them, and the middle lines as a triumphant taunt of death. Others read the opening as questions, asking whether God will ransom them from Sheol and redeem them from Death, with the answer no, and the middle lines as God calling Death to bring its plagues against Israel. The last line, compassion is hidden from God's eyes, and the verses on either side, which are all judgment, support the threatening reading in its setting.

The promising reading draws strength from Hosea's habit of sudden turns to hope (11:8-9; 14:4) and from Paul's use of the verse. Some interpreters hold both together: in the short run God will not spare Samaria, but his final purpose is to defeat death itself. Readers can see that the immediate sense is disputed while seeing why the church has heard good news in it.
passages.asks: Israel trusted kings who could not save it. Ask what you have trusted to save you that cannot. And Paul heard in this verse God's last word over death. Ask what it would mean for you if death does not have the last word.

passages.t: The east wind, and the fall of Samaria
passages.happening:
Though Ephraim flourishes among his brothers, an east wind will come, a wind from the LORD rising from the desert (verse 15). His spring will fail and his fountain run dry, and his treasury will be plundered of everything precious.

‘Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword’ (verse 16). The rest of the verse names the cruelties of war that will fall on the city's children and its pregnant women. These notes name them and do not describe them.
passages.hearers:
The east wind was the hot, dry wind from the desert that withered everything it touched. Here it stands for Assyria, the power from the east that would sweep over Israel.

Verse 16, numbered 14:1 in the Hebrew Bible, describes the fall of Samaria. It came in 722 BC after a siege of about three years by the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V, with the deportations completed under his successor, Sargon II. The site's guide to the kings, following Thiele's dates, gives 723 or 722 BC. The cruelties the verse names were common in ancient conquest, and the prophets name them as crimes when others commit them.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the siege and the fall: ‘In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria’ (2 Kings 17:6). Amos names the same cruelty as a crime of the Ammonites in Gilead (Amos 1:13).
passages.hard:
How should the end of this chapter be read?

Hosea is not approving the cruelty he names. He is warning his own people of what invasion will bring, and the prophets condemn such acts as crimes when other nations commit them. This is a theological reading of a political disaster, written in Israel's own Scripture, spoken by an Israelite prophet to his own nation. It gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved, or to point this verse at anyone else. And it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now. The next verse begins Hosea's last call to return.

A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. Your loss was not a judgment on you. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he refused that reading of a disaster: “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying this, you need people more than explanations. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: Ephraim flourished, and the east wind came anyway. Ask what you are counting on that a single wind could dry up. And ask how you can hold the warning of this verse for yourself without ever pointing it at someone else's pain.
